title: Egyptian Arabic
text:
Egyptian Arabic
These are my study notes structured as a path into spoken Egyptian Arabic (العامية المصرية)

title: Egyptian Arabic
text:
How to use it

Arabic is always visible. Wherever you see a sentence, you can tap it to reveal its franco (Latin-letter transcription) and its English meaning. Try to read the Arabic first.
Franco uses the Egyptian number system, where a few digits stand in for sounds with no Latin letter: 2 = ء/ق · 3 = ع · 7 = ح · 5 = خ · 8 = غ. The emphatic letters (ص، ط، ض) are written as plain s, t, d.
Two tracks, move freely between them. The Grammar chapters explain how the language works — verb types, the article, negation, and so on. The Conversation chapters put the language to use around a theme and the vocabulary that comes with it. The conversation chapters don’t wait for the grammar; when you want the mechanics behind something, jump to the matching grammar chapter.

title: Egyptian Arabic
text:
Part I — Grammar
The reference track: how Egyptian Arabic is built.

G1 · Sentences without “to be” — pronouns, gender, and the mesh negation
G2 · The definite article and agreement — el-… el-…: “the red book” vs “the book is red”
G3 · Verbs in the present — the بـ prefix, the verb types (sound, hollow, final-weak, doubled, reflexive), and the participle
G4 · Verbs in the past — the suffix conjugation, type by type
G5 · Verbs in the future — the هـ prefix
G6 · Negation — mesh vs the wrapped ma…sh
G7 · Adverbs — time, place, frequency, manner
G8 · The bare imperfect — the “subjunctive” form after 3ayez, lazem, momken
G9 · Conditionals — sentences with law

title: Egyptian Arabic
text:
Part II — Conversation
The thematic track: each chapter brings a topic and the words that live with it.

C1 · Greetings and politeness
C2 · Introducing yourself — name, origin, age, and the question words
C3 · This and that — the objects around you (clothes, furniture, animals)
C4 · Colors and sizes — describing things
C5 · Liking, wanting, disliking (حب / عايز / بكره) — food, drink, eating and drinking
C6 · Work (اشتغل) — jobs and the places you work
C7 · Studying and learning (اتعلم) — languages, music, instruments, culture
C8 · Speaking and understanding (اتكلم / فهم)
C9 · Knowing and being acquainted (عرف)
C10 · Movement (راح / جه / رجع) — going, directions, and places
C11 · The daily routine — waking, sleeping, meals, telling the time
C12 · Saying, telling, hearing (قال / حكى / سمع) — reported speech


New chapters are added one at a time. A ✓ in the sidebar means a chapter is ready; the rest are on the way.

title: The Arabic Alphabet
text:
Introduction
The Arabic alphabet has 28 letters and is written right to left. Most letters change shape depending on where they sit in the word:

Isolated — the letter on its own
Initial — at the start of a word
Medial — in the middle
Final — at the end

A few letters don’t join to the letter that follows them, so they only have two shapes (isolated/final and initial/medial).

title: The Arabic Alphabet
text:
Special letters

Hamza — ء
The hamza isn’t a true letter but a mark for a glottal stop. It can stand alone or sit on/under another letter:

ء — hamza on its own
أ — hamza over alif
إ — hamza under alif
ؤ — hamza over waaw
ئ — hamza over yaa

Examples: سؤال - so2al - question · أنا - ana - I · شيء - shay2 - thing · قرأ - 2ara - read



Taa Marbuta — ة
This appears only at the end of a word and usually marks the feminine:

ة — taa marbuta (isolated / final)

Examples: مدرسة - madrasa - school · ساعة - sa3a - hour / clock · جامعة - gam3a - university · كويسة - kwayesa - good (f.)

title: The Arabic Alphabet
text:
Special joining: Laam-Alif — لا
When ل (laam) meets ا (alif), they form a special ligature:

لا — laa

Examples: لا - la2 - no · لازم - lazem - it’s necessary / must · ولا - walla - or

title: The Arabic Alphabet
text:
Vowels and diacritics
Written Arabic normally leaves out the short vowels. They can be shown with marks (rarely used in modern texts):

Short vowels

َ◌ (fat7a) — short “a”
ِ◌ (kasra) — short “i”
ُ◌ (damma) — short “u”



Long vowels

ا (alif) — “aa”
ي (yaa) — “ee” / “ii”
و (waaw) — “oo” / “uu”



Other marks

ْ◌ (sukoon) — no vowel
ّ◌ (shadda) — doubles the letter
ً◌ (tanween) — an “-an” ending

title: The Arabic Alphabet
text:
Tips for learning

Letters that don’t join to the next one: ا د ذ ر ز و — they only have two shapes (isolated/final).
Look-alikes (told apart by the dots):

ب (1 dot below) · ت (2 dots above) · ث (3 dots above)
ج (1 dot below) · ح (no dot) · خ (1 dot above)
د (no dot) · ذ (1 dot above)
ر (no dot) · ز (1 dot above)
س (no dots) · ش (3 dots above)
ص (no dot) · ض (1 dot above)
ط (no dot) · ظ (1 dot above)
ع (no dot) · غ (1 dot above)

Practice: first learn to recognize the isolated letters, then the joined shapes.
Writing: practice writing right to left, joining letters where they connect.

title: The Arabic Alphabet
text:
The franco (Arabizi) system
Some Arabic sounds have no Latin letter, so numbers stand in for them:

2 = ء / ق (hamza / Egyptian qaaf) — a glottal stop
3 = ع (3ain) — a throaty voiced sound
5 = خ (khaa) — like Spanish “j” / Scottish “loch”
7 = ح (7aa) — a breathy throat “h”
8 = غ (ghain) — like a French/German “r”


A few Egyptian notes

ق (qaaf) in Egypt is usually pronounced 2 (a glottal stop): qahwa → 2ahwa.
El before a word = “the”.
W + vowel contracts: we + inta → winta.
Countries are always feminine.
Ya before a name is an informal vocative: ya Salma = “hey Salma”.

8. Comparativos — أفعل (afʻal)

Estrutura
Em árabe egípcio, o comparativo usa o padrão أَفْعَل (afʻal) + من (min = “do que”):

title: This and That
text:
How it works
This chapter teaches the words for pointing at things: this / that — ده (da), دي (di) and دول (dol) — and how to name the objects around you. Tap any sentence to reveal its franco and English.
One set covers both “this” and “that”. Egyptian doesn’t split them: ده (da) for a masculine thing, دي (di) for a feminine thing, دول (dol) for plural — used for near and far alike. A gesture or the word هناك (henak) “there” marks distance when you need it.
Two structures, and the contrast matters:
So el-ketab da (this book) and da ketab (this is a book) are different sentences — watch the word order.
Asking: ده إيه؟ (da eh?) / دي إيه؟ (di eh?) = “what’s this?”.
Whose is it — بتاع (betaa3). To say “mine / yours”, use بتاع, which agrees with the thing owned and then takes an ending: الكتاب ده بتاعي (el-ketab da bta3i) “this book is mine”; for a feminine thing, بتاعتي (bta3ti).

title: This and That
text:
After a noun (the noun takes ال): الكتاب ده (el-ketab da) = “this book”. Here the demonstrative is just describing.
At the front, as the subject: ده كتاب (da ketab) = “this is a book”. Egyptian has no verb “to be”, so the bare demonstrative + noun already means “this is…”.

title: The Present Tense
text:
The بـ prefix
A grammar chapter that pulls together the present tense you’ve been meeting verb by verb. Three things to take away: the بـ prefix, the four personal prefixes, and the fact that verbs come in types that share one set of endings. Tap any example to reveal its franco and English.
A bare present verb in Egyptian carries a بـ (bi‑) in front. That prefix is what marks an everyday present — a habit or something going on right now:
Drop the بـ and you get the bare form used after words like عايز (want), لازم (must) and ممكن (can) — 3ayez aroo7 “I want to go”. That bare form has its own grammar chapter; here everything keeps its بـ.

text:
The participle
Not everything “happening now” is a بـ verb. For states — wanting, knowing, going, living — Egyptian often uses a participle: an adjective-like word that agrees in gender and number and takes no بـ.

text:
The one complication: hollow verbs
Regular verbs keep their stem unchanged. Hollow verbs (the ones with a long vowel in the middle — راح، نام، شاف) do something special: in front of a consonant suffix the long vowel shortens. Watch راح (raa7) “to go”:

The split is clean: هو، هي، هم keep the long vowel (raa7‑); everyone else takes the short one (ro7‑). The same happens with نام → نمت (nemt) and شاف → شفت (shoft).

title: Negation
text:
The rule in one line
Egyptian has two ways to say “not”, and choosing between them comes down to one question: is the thing you’re negating a verb or not? Tap any example to reveal its franco and English.

title: Negation
text:
Not a verb (a noun, adjective, participle, place) → put مش (mesh) in front.
A verb (present or past) → wrap ما…ش (ma…sh) around it.

title: Negation
section: مش — for everything that isn’t a verb
text:
مش — for everything that isn’t a verb
Nominal sentences, adjectives, participles, prepositional phrases — all take a single مش in front of the negated part.


أنا مش دكتور

ana mesh doktor I’m not a doctor (nominal)



الأكل مش حلو

el-akl mesh 7elw the food isn’t nice (adjective)



مش عايز قهوة

mesh 3ayez 2ahwa I don’t want coffee (participle)



أنا مش هنا

ana mesh hena I’m not here (place)

Remember the participle catch from the present-tense chapter: عايز، عارف، فاهم look like “I want / know / understand”, but they’re not verbs, so they take مش — never ما…ش.

title: Introductions
text:
Two patterns that run through it all
Everything you need to meet someone: ask their name, where they’re from, how old they are, whether they work or study. It reuses the verbs you already know (اشتغل، درس، اتكلم، اتعلم) — so here we ask the questions and let those chapters carry the conjugations. Tap any example to reveal its franco and English.
(The بـ on the present-tense verbs below is explained in the Present Tense chapter.)

title: Introductions
text:
Question words go at the END. esmak eh? is literally “your-name what?”, inta feen? is “you where?”. That’s the normal order, not an emphatic one.
There is no “to have”. Egyptian uses عند (3and) plus an ending — and the very same word does age: 3andak kam sana? is literally “you have how many years?”.

text:
The pattern
How to say one thing is bigger / smaller / smarter than another. Egyptian has a tidy pattern for it, and one feature that makes it easier than the adjectives you already know. Tap any example to reveal its franco and English.
Take an adjective, reshape it into the أفعل (af3al) mould, and follow it with من (men) “than”:
[subject] + [أفعل form] + من + [the thing compared]

The easy part: it doesn’t agree
Ordinary adjectives change for gender — tawil (m.) becomes tawila (f.). The comparative does not. The أفعل form is invariable: it’s atwal whether you’re talking about a man, a woman, or a crowd.

Numbers
A grammar-plus-vocabulary chapter: how Egyptian counts, how nouns go plural, and the everyday calendar words — parts of the day, days of the week, the time adverbs, and the months. Tap any example to reveal its franco and English.
The base numbers (you also met these telling the time in the Daily Routine chapter):

“X is [somewhere] Y”
Because there’s no verb “to be” (the Pronouns chapter), saying where something is takes no verb at all. Just line up [thing] + [place word] + [the place]:

title: Prepositions and Place Words
text:
في and من — “in / at” and “from”
These two carry most of your location work.

في (fi) = in / at: ana fi el-bet “I’m at home”, bashta8al fi maktab “I work in an office”.
من (men) = from: ana men masr “I’m from Egypt”.

A note worth keeping: with a verb of motion you often need no preposition at all for the destination — baroo7 el-sho8l is simply “I go (to) work”, with no word for “to”.

title: Prepositions and Place Words
section: لـ and ليه — a pair to keep apart
text:
لـ and ليه — a pair to keep apart
They look almost the same but do completely different jobs:

لـ (le) = to / for / until — el-hedeyya le Mona “the gift is for Mona”, men el-sa3a talata le el-5amsa “from three to five”.
ليه (leeh) = why — a question word: betet3allim 3araby leeh? “why are you learning Arabic?”.

One is a little preposition glued to the next word; the other is a full question word that lands at the end of the sentence.

Personal pronouns

title: Pronouns and the Nominal Sentence
text:
The sentence without “to be”
Egyptian has no present-tense verb “to be”. You just place the two parts side by side — I + a doctor — and the “am” is understood.


أنا دكتور

ana doktor I’m a doctor (literally just “I doctor”)

To say “is not”, put مش (mesh) in front of the second part:


أنا مش جاهز

ana mesh gahez I’m not ready

(This مش is for non-verb sentences. Negating an actual verb uses the wrapped ما…ش — that’s its own grammar chapter.)

title: Pronouns and the Nominal Sentence
text:
Gender
Almost everything is either masculine or feminine, and it shows up on adjectives:

A noun ending in ة (‑a) is usually feminine: madrasa (school), sa3a (watch).
Adjectives agree — the feminine adds ة: kbeer / kbeera (big), masri / masreyya (Egyptian).
Countries are feminine: masr (Egypt) takes feminine agreement — masr 7elwa “Egypt is beautiful”.

title: Saying, Telling, Hearing
text:
How it works
This chapter gathers three verbs of communication: to say (قال — 2al), to tell / recount (حكى — 7aka) and to hear / listen (سمع — seme3). Together they let you report what other people said and heard. Tap any sentence to reveal its franco and English.
Three verbs, three shapes you’ve already met. قال is a hollow verb — exactly like راح from the movement chapter (2al / yi2ool / 2olt). حكى is final-weak, like مشي (7aka / yi7ki / 7akeet). سمع is a plain regular verb, like فهم (seme3 / yisma3 / seme3t). If those felt familiar, these will too.
The thread is reported speech with إن (inn) = “that”. You hook a whole clause onto the verb: قال إن… (2al inn…) “he said that…”, سمعت إن… (seme3t inn…) “I heard that…”.
Which verb when? اتكلم (from the speaking chapter) is to speak / talk in general. قال is to say — specific words or a “that”-clause. حكى is to tell / recount — a story or what happened. سمع is to hear / listen.
Saying it to someone. A short pronoun attaches to the verb: قالّي (2alli) “he told me”, قلتلك (2oltelak) “I told you”, حكتلي (7aket-li) “she told me”.

title: Speaking and Understanding
text:
How it works
These are two of the first verbs you’ll ever need: to speak (اتكلم — itkallim) and to understand (فهم — fehem). “I speak a little Arabic” and “I don’t understand” come up on day one. Tap any sentence to reveal its franco and English.
The present and past you already know: بـ for the present (batkallim = “I speak”), endings for the past (itkallimt = “I spoke”). The future is just ها + the present stem without بـ: hatkallim (“I’ll speak”), hafham (“I’ll understand”).
Understanding likes the participle. Just like raye7 / gayy from the movement lessons, the verb فهم has an adjective-like form فاهم (fahim) that you use for the state of understanding right now. “I understand” is far more often أنا فاهم (ana fahim) than the full present bafham. Its negative, مش فاهم (mesh fahim) = “I don’t understand”, is one of the most useful phrases in the language.
Two ways to say “not”. With the participle, put مش in front: mesh fahim. With the verb itself, wrap it in ما…ش: mabatkallimsh = “I don’t speak”, mafhemtesh = “I didn’t understand”.

title: Knowing and Being Acquainted
text:
How it works
One verb, عرف (3eref), does a lot of work. This lesson keeps the grammar light and instead widens the vocabulary you can plug into it. Tap any sentence to reveal its franco and English.
One verb for saber and conhecer. Portuguese splits “sei a resposta” from “conheço o Ahmed”, but Arabic doesn’t: عرف covers knowing a fact, knowing a person, and knowing a place. One verb, three jobs.
It also loves the participle — exactly like فاهم from the last lesson. The state “I know” is normally أنا عارف (ana 3aref), not the full present. The past verb 3eref leans toward “found out / came to know”; the participle 3aref is “I know it now”. Its negative مش عارف (mesh 3aref) = “I don’t know” (you’ll also hear the verb form معرفش, ma3rafsh).
عرف + a verb = “to know how to / to be able to”. Follow عرف with a bare present verb (no بـ): بعرف أسوق (ba3raf asoo2) = “I know how to drive / I can drive”. This is how Egyptian says “can” without a separate verb.

title: Verbs of Movement 1: Go, Come, Return
text:
How movement works
This lesson builds the three everyday verbs — go (راح), come (جه) and return (رجع) — plus the basic words for near and far and the prepositions you need to say where you’re heading. Tap any sentence to reveal its franco and English.
Three tense markers. Egyptian Arabic glues a prefix onto the verb to mark tense. The present takes بـ (be-) for a habit or an action happening now (baru7 = “I go / I’m going”). The future takes هـ (ha-) (haru7 = “I’ll go”). The past has no prefix — it uses endings instead (ro7t = “I went”).
The three verbs are three different shapes, and the shape tells you what to expect. راح (go) is a hollow verb — its middle root letter (و) shifts around, so ro7t (“I went”) barely resembles ra7 (“he went”). جه (come) is irregular — its present ييجي looks unrelated to its past جه, so just memorise both. رجع (return) is a regular sound verb — the stem stays put (rege3 / yirga3), making it the easiest of the three.
The participle — your most useful shortcut. Instead of the full present, Egyptians very often use an adjective-like form to say “(I’m) on my way”: رايح (raye7) going, جاي (gayy) coming, راجع (rage3) heading back. It agrees in gender and number, and it’s how you actually say “I’m coming!” — ana gayy!
Saying where. Use لـ (le) = “to”, or just drop in the bare place (raye7 esh-sho8l = “going to work”). من (men) = “from”.

title: Liking, Wanting, Disliking
text:
How it works
This chapter is about taste and preference: to like / love (بحب — ba7ebb), to want (عايز — 3ayez) and to hate (بكره — bakrah), plus the food and drink you’ll use them on. Tap any sentence to reveal its franco and English.
حب is one verb for both like and love (like saber/conhecer being one verb). It’s a doubled verb (ح-ب-ب): بحب (ba7ebb). Negate it by wrapping it in ما…ش: مبحبش (maba7ebbesh) “I don’t like”.
عايز (“want”) just agrees — it’s not conjugated and takes no بـ: 3ayez (m.), 3ayza (f.), 3ayzeen (pl.). Negate with مش (mesh).
بكره (bakrah) = “to hate / detest” — a regular verb (ك-ر-ه), negated with ما…ش (مبكرهش, mabkrahsh).
The intensity scale. Egyptian has a clear ladder of feeling, from adoring to hating:
بموت في literally means “I die for” — use it for the thing you adore: bamoot fi el-shokolata.
And remember the demonstratives from the last chapter: بحب ده (ba7ebb da) “I like this”, بكره ده (bakrah da) “I hate that”.

title: Colors
text:
How it works
Now we add color, reusing حب (like) and عايز (want) from the last lesson. The one new idea: in Arabic a color is an adjective that agrees with its noun. Tap any sentence to reveal its franco and English.
The basic colors have a masculine and a feminine form. A masculine noun takes the a‑ form, a feminine noun takes the ‑a form: القلم الأحمر (el-2alam el-a7mar) = “the red pen”, but العربية الحمرا (el-3arabeyya el-7amra) = “the red car”. As with any adjective, the noun and the color both carry the article: el-2alam el-azra2.
The “derived” colors don’t change. Colors that end in ‑i — bonny (brown), ramadi (grey), borto2ani (orange), bambi (pink) — stay the same for masculine and feminine.

title: Colors and Sizes
text:
How it works
Now we describe things by their color (لون — loon) and size. This builds directly on the article rule from the grammar chapter: an adjective follows its noun and matches it. Tap any sentence to reveal its franco and English.
Basic colors come in a pair — a masculine a‑ form and a feminine ‑a form: أحمر (a7mar) / حمرا (7amra). The “derived” colors that end in ‑i (bonni, ramadi…) take ‑eyya in the feminine (bonneyya), though in everyday speech they’re often left unchanged.
Sizes work the same way — a masculine and a feminine form: kebir / kebira.
Definiteness still applies (from the grammar chapter): if the noun has ال, the color or size takes ال too — الفستان الأحمر (el-fustan el-a7mar) “the red dress”. Drop the article from the adjective and you get a sentence: الفستان أحمر (el-fustan a7mar) “the dress is red”.
Stacking color + size: put both after the noun, each with ال if the noun is definite — الفستان الأحمر الطويل (el-fustan el-a7mar el-tawil) “the long red dress”.

title: The Definite Article and Agreement
text:
The article: ال (el-)
A grammar chapter. It covers the definite article ال (el-) = “the”, one rule that surprises every learner, and a small trick that turns a phrase into a full sentence. Tap any example to reveal its franco and English.
“The” is ال, glued onto the front of the word: البيت (el-bet) = “the house”, القلم (el-2alam) = “the pen”. There’s no separate word for “a / an” — a noun with no ال is simply indefinite: bet = “a house”.

title: The Definite Article and Agreement
text:
The rule that surprises everyone
An adjective comes after its noun and matches its definiteness. So if the noun is definite (has ال), the adjective takes ال too. Portuguese says “the” once; Arabic repeats it on every word of the phrase — literally “the dress the red”.

The trick: how a phrase becomes “is”
Arabic has no verb “to be” in the present. This makes one tiny difference do a lot of work: if the noun is definite but the adjective is bare (no ال), the adjective stops describing and becomes a predicate — it means “is”.

الفستان أحمر

el-fustan a7mar the dress is red (a full sentence — only the noun has ال)

To negate that sentence, put مش (mesh) before the adjective:

title: The Definite Article and Agreement
text:
A note on pronunciation: “sun letters”
In writing, ال is always ال. But in speech, the ل blends into certain following consonants (the “sun letters”: t, d, s, sh, z, r, n, l…). So الشمس looks like el-shams but is said esh-shams, and السمك is said es-samak. Before other letters (“moon letters”) the l stays: البيت is el-bet. We keep writing el- throughout this book for simplicity — just know that your ear will often hear the next letter doubled instead.

title: Everyday Verbs
text:
How it works
A handful of very common verbs that don’t belong to one theme but show up everywhere: to see / watch (شوف — shaaf), to take (أخد — a5ad), to ask (سأل — sa2al), to need (احتاج — e7tag) and to write (كتب — katab). Tap any sentence to reveal its franco and English.
These five between them cover most of the verb types you’ve already met: شوف is hollow (like راح), كتب and سأل are regular (like فهم), أخد is a little irregular, and احتاج runs like اشتغل. As always, the future is ها + the stem, and the past uses endings.
A few patterns worth noting:

احتاج takes either a thing or another verb: ba7tag mosa3da “I need help”, ba7tag aroo7 “I need to go”.
سأل pairs with عن (3an) “about”: bas2al 3an el-mudeer “I ask about the manager”.
شوف covers see, watch and look.

text:
How the future works
In Egyptian Arabic, the present and the future share the same verb stem and the same personal prefixes. The only thing that changes is the particle at the front of the verb:
So to build the future, take the present, drop the بـ, and add هـ. The personal prefixes (a-, te-, ye-, ne-) stay exactly the same — only the front particle changes. (Some people write the future with حـ ḥa- instead of هـ; they mean the same thing.)

title: “بكرة هنعمل إيه؟ — The future tense (practice)”
text:
The present uses بـ (bi-) for habits and ongoing actions — أنا بسافر (ana basafir) = “I travel / I’m travelling”.
The future uses هـ (ha-) for plans and intentions — أنا هسافر (ana hasafir) = “I will travel”.
